claims.text: Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloy systems can be used to produce a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Conventional alloys are the relevant initial material state.
Replacing conventional alloys with compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys changes the alloy composition in a way relevant to the transition.
The relevant behavior occurs within a narrow temperature window.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys possess temper-embrittlement resistance.
Temper-embrittlement resistance leads to a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Conventional alloys exhibiting temper embrittlement provide the baseline.

contradictions.description: Temper-embrittlement resistance implies avoidance of an embrittled state, whereas a ductile–brittle–ductile transition requires an intervening brittle state; no alternative mechanism reconciles these statements.

The predicted ductile–brittle–ductile transition necessarily entails a loss of ductility in an intermediate temperature interval, but the falsification rule treats a significant loss of ductility in that interval as falsifying the hypothesis.
